title: Benet Devereux: Seeking Treasure in the Tangled Bank: Biological Inspiration for Roguelike Me
speaker: Benet Devereux
summary: Benet Devereux argues that biology, where complexity emerges from simple interacting agents, is a rich source of roguelike mechanics. Starting from a small rot.js game about a tardigrade surviving extreme conditions by going dormant, he browsed the biomimicry catalog at asknature.org and abstracted organism strategies into game ideas. Examples include a smell-based sensory layer inspired by desert ants, cone snails mixing venom cocktails to target a victim's vulnerability, and an invisible anglerfish with a lure. He frames these as quick idea generation rather than finished designs, and notes many strategies depend on physics too rich for most games.

insights.claim: Biology, where complex diversity emerges from agents following simple principles, can be read as a manifesto for procedural generation and a source of roguelike mechanics.
insights.detail: Devereux takes Darwin's 'tangled bank' passage as his title and flips it: if complexity from simplicity is nature's process, it can also be a design goal, so in a sense biology is roguelike.
insights.quote: let's put complexity from simplicity as a design goal which in a way I think turns this into a bit of a manifesto for procedural generation

insights.claim: Devereux's small tardigrade roguelike built its whole design around the animal's most famous ability, going dormant to survive extremes, so the goal became surviving a set time and the rest of the design was generating extreme situations.
insights.detail: He made the game to learn rot.js and wanted the player character's mechanics and narrative to be tardigrade-inspired.
insights.quote: the goal became survival and surviving for a set amount of time in extreme situations

insights.claim: To turn real organism strategies into mechanics you must abstract, by asking what resources matter to each actor, what senses they use and how they interact, and the resulting strategy must be a meaningful choice rather than a button to keep smashing.
insights.detail: Devereux notes no game can present every situation an organism faces. He used asknature.org's taxonomy of strategies, meant for real-world engineers, as an idea generator for creating problems in an imaginary world, with overlapping buckets such as defense and deception or navigation and resource gathering.
insights.quote: consider what resources matter to different actors in the game, what the different sensory modalties to actors are

insights.claim: A smell map as a separate sensory modality, inspired by foraging desert ants, could let a character detect unseen threats, with scents that mask each other or wash off unlike line of sight.
insights.detail: Devereux's illustrations: the player smells the acid of a green dragon in a far corridor it cannot see, but a fresh smelly corpse in the room masks the dragon's scent so the player might walk into danger.
insights.quote: player character is able to smell the acid from a green dragon lurking in the far corridor that it can't see

insights.claim: Cone snails suggest a monster that mixes a custom venom cocktail for each target, choosing toxins that exploit the specific victim's vulnerability.
insights.detail: Some cone snail species tailor their venom to the prey. Devereux's illustration shows a cone snail delivering a paralyzing toxin combined with white dragon venom aimed at the player character's weakness.
insights.quote: It is delivering a paraalizing toxin with white dragon venom which targets this PC's vulnerability

insights.claim: The anglerfish suggests an invisible ambush monster with a visible lure that draws prey in, and whose light can also spoil the player's dark adaptation if that is a mechanic.
insights.detail: Devereux notes the anglerfish's skin is non-reflective and black, so prey cannot see it even by the lure's light. Host Alexei relays chat's view that a mimic with a lure adds a layer to the familiar mimic idea.
insights.quote: it can make it harder for prey animals to see in the dark. If you have dark adaptation as a game mechanic

insights.claim: Many biological strategies are hard to use in games because they rely on form and material properties that would need a rich physics engine.
insights.detail: Devereux discarded many ideas for this reason. He lists resource constraints and complex collective behaviour of organisms as promising unexplored avenues.
insights.quote: they really rely a lot on form and material properties and require like a pretty rich physics engine
